<description>
{
 "summary": "Makes `Ipc::disconnectIncoming` disconnect incoming connections and wait off the event loop thread for in-flight server call bodies to complete before returning during shutdown. Updates libmultiprocess to split connection teardown from destruction, track active server objects across worker threads, and provide a `waitDrained` barrier. Also incorporates libmultiprocess fixes for connection cleanup races, listener capacity accounting, and thread map use-after-free bugs.",
 "problem": "When a node shuts down while an IPC client is executing an asynchronous method (such as an IPC miner calling `Mining.checkBlock`), canceling network promises does not stop C++ method bodies already running on worker threads. Those worker threads continue running and dereference node state (such as `m_node.chainman`) after `Shutdown()` has cleared it, causing assertion failures and process crashes.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"This fixes an antithesis bug reported in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35845 and similar bug reported in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33387 where if asynchronous IPC mining calls are made when the node is shutting down it's possible for assert(m_node.chainman) to trigger.\"",
  "Commit dc293af2f43: \"Disconnecting cancels the KJ promise of an in-flight IPC server call, but a C++ server method body already dispatched to a libmultiprocess worker thread is not interrupted and runs to completion. A still-running body (an in-flight Mining.checkBlock) could then dereference m_node.chainman after chainman.reset() nulled it, aborting on Assert(m_node.chainman).\""
 ],
 "dependencies": {

<category name="ipc" title="IPC / multiprocess">
## Covers

The process-separation project and everything that serves it: the
`interfaces::` abstraction layer between node, wallet, and GUI, the Cap'n
Proto interface definitions and generated-code machinery, the
libmultiprocess subtree, the `bitcoin-node` / `bitcoin-gui` /
`bitcoin-wallet` executables and the `bitcoin` wrapper, IPC process
management (spawning, connecting, disconnect handling), and the tests and
build glue for all of it. The IPC label is a strong prior.

Not ipc: PRs whose subject is what the mining interface exposes or how
templates are built (category `mining`), even though they travel over
IPC. A mining PR is ipc only if it changes IPC infrastructure itself
(serialization, connection handling, the capnp toolchain). Likewise a
wallet or GUI PR that adds a method to `interfaces::Wallet` is wallet
first; it is ipc only if the interface mechanics are the point.

A general-utility PR (a result type, a logging helper) that the
multiprocess stack happens to be based on is not ipc.

## What matters here

Anything that lets external software use the node over IPC reliably: the
stability and completeness of the mining interface and its consumers,
crash and disconnect handling, correctness of serialization across the
process boundary, and platform coverage (the IPC binaries building and
passing tests on every supported platform). Then progress on running the
wallet and GUI as separate processes, which is the project's stated goal.
Then reductions in the maintenance burden of the interface layer:
generated code, build integration, the libmultiprocess subtree sync.

Interface cleanups without a consumer waiting on them are P3 or below.

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.
